notes: A covers part of the key: aim for under 10% churn and track churn by cohort because month-1 churn is highest. But its SaaS-style table calls anything over 15% broken, which contradicts the Skool platform average of 20% churn. B's quotes all appear in ./raw/, but it wrongly says its sources have no churn benchmark (yt--j8_YCWZ05Q gives the 80% retention and day-90 figures), so it misses Hormozi's actual position entirely.

Both answers pick revenue share and give the reason that the client controls profit, but neither cites his actual points ('top line's top line', paid in proportion to risk, the six-deal ranking). B wins narrowly because its quotes are real ones I found in ./raw/. A credits Hormozi with generic sayings like 'revenue is vanity, profit is sanity'. B is weakened by falsely saying the sources don't cover rev vs. profit share and by stretching the partner-fraud story to fit.

Both answers land on 'bootstrap' and neither mentions ignorance debt or the management, technical and data debt that bootstrapping piles up. A's quotes check out in ./raw/ and are more specific to Hormozi, but its central claim that the sources never address this question is false: yt-sL16tsGafcQ covers it directly. B states the key's position more cleanly ('raise only if the business can't work without it') and gives the user a more usable decision test.

Neither answer gives the 4-4-4 promotion/delivery/building split or the 111 rule. A's day starts with lead generation and then moves to sales and delivery, which is close to his 'promotion first' order, and it gives a concrete schedule. B's quotes do appear in ./raw, but it wrongly says the sources never describe how he structures a workday, and its 'no fixed end time' advice is less practical.

Neither answer reaches Hormozi's actual position. He says to pay it off: he skews 'very close to the Ramsey side' because debt adds risk that tends to come due over time. A falls into the generic rate-versus-return trap, but it leans toward paying the debt down, keeping a reserve and growing only through proven channels. B says the sources don't cover debt (they do) and concludes he'd 'keep the cash and grow', which contradicts his stated view. B's quotes are mostly real, but that conclusion misrepresents him.

B gets Hormozi's core position right: keep running a winning hook 'to death' and only try to beat it. I checked its main quotes against raw/yt-JDR-R--4HhM.md and they are real, though it misses the key's specifics (School Games copy run for 6 months, three hooks over 5 years, kaleidoscoping creative). A has a 'don't kill a winner' point, but its plan of weekly hook batches and new angles every 2–4 weeks is essentially the generic trap, and none of its Hormozi points are tied to a source.

Both say to raise prices because an 82% close rate is high, and both include break-even math. Neither mentions that a higher price can raise the customer's belief that you can deliver. B grounds its advice in real Hormozi quotes, which I checked in ./raw/: 'middle is where people die', 'confront the high price' and 'sausage making'. A paraphrases him and leans toward the generic advice to test cautiously. A point against B: it wrongly claims no source covers close rate.

Both answers get the main call right: keep knocking doors and don't start ads yet. Both then miss the key's central point, which is to build volume on repairs and raise the repair ticket to $2.5-5k, and both partly fall into the trap of steering toward replacements (B goes further and makes replacements 'the one thing'). B's quotes are real ones found in ./raw/, but they come from general talks, not the roofing video. A is clearer and more actionable, and its door-volume reasoning is closer to the key's 'go all in on door-to-door'.

A comes closer to the key: it uses 'More, Better, New', calls creative volume (including UGC creators) a likely cause of the wall, and tells the user to keep Meta as the engine. It still slips into the generic advice to diversify into affiliates and podcasts. B's quotes check out in ./raw/, but it frames the fix as the offer and money model, not creative, and it never names creative as the main limit.

A gets Hormozi's core position right: overwhelm drives churn, so cut back instead of adding. It backs this with real, verifiable quotes from the Skool Games case. It misses the 30%→5% Skool churn figure and the 16-17% annual discount, and it says wrongly that he never addresses 'too expensive' (he says to add a cheaper tier only if ideal customers cite price). B lands roughly on 'subtract' but stays generic, offers a pause or maintenance tier to everyone, and credits Hormozi with quotes that look made up.
